I have a vague philosophy around the idea that most if not all work can be divided into two simple categories: do you work for people who can afford what you provide, or for people who need it? I don't necessarily mean simply who signs the cheques or who receives the immediate product of your work, but rather to spur thinking about what the actual concept of work means to a given person, if there are different opportunities to serve someone else's needs, and maybe lead to outcomes such as better understanding of people's motivations or what would constitute a satisfying career for an individual. I absolutely don't mean to imply that someone's moral standing should be lessened by doing work for the pay instead of for the good it does the world. Choosing what we do for a living is a privilege that varies wildly from person to person and place to place, we all know that. I just think this can be a useful framework for thinking about how to distribute our attention and energy to sustainable and rewarding lives, which I think is crucial if we're to ever improve the world the way we dream of.

Pro tip: beans in a baked potato is an excellent combo because it covers protein, carbs and fiber without too much fat. It's worth noting that the skin of the potato contains much of its nutrients and fiber. In fact, let me talk for a second about the role of fiber in a healthy diet. 

When ingested with carbs, (e.g. rice or potatoes), fiber slows down the digestion of said carbs, allowing them to enter your bloodstream as glucose more gradually than if you just ate the carbs on their own. This is the difference between a sugar rush and a good meal that keeps you energized for longer. The short term effect of eating carbs without fiber is an energy spike followed by a crash, and the long term effect is often weight gain. For more on this concept, do some cursory research on the glycemic index, also sometimes known as "fast vs slow carbs". For people eating on a budget it can be easy and tempting to just live off of white rice and call it good, but a little better understanding of how the body converts food to energy can go a long way toward a healthy life.
